opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That question is really the heart of the work we did with my students, Rylan Schaeffer and Brando Miranda. Our short answer is that a lot of what's been called emergence depends heavily on how you measure it, more than on some fundamental change in the model.

The setup is this. People had been reporting "emergent abilities": capabilities that seem absent in smaller models and then appear sharply, almost unpredictably, once you pass some scale. That's a striking claim. If it's true, it matters for safety and planning, because you can't forecast what the next model will do. So we asked whether that sharpness lives in the model or in the yardstick.

What we found is that many of these results use metrics that are nonlinear or discontinuous in the model's underlying per-token performance. Exact match is the classic example. If you're scoring multi-digit arithmetic and the model has to get every token right, then even if its per-token accuracy is improving smoothly and predictably with scale, the probability of getting the whole string right stays near zero for a long time. Then it shoots up. Plot that against model size and it looks like a phase transition.

When you take the same model outputs and score them with a continuous metric, like token edit distance or the probability assigned to the correct answer, the curve often becomes smooth and predictable. Nothing changed about the models; only the measurement did.

We tested this in a few ways:

- **Reanalysis:** we went back to existing model families and showed the emergence largely disappears under continuous metrics.
- **Benchmark survey:** we looked across benchmarks and found that claims of emergence concentrate on a small number of metrics, mostly the harsh, all-or-nothing ones.
- **Induced emergence:** we showed you can create apparent emergence in vision models, where nobody had claimed it, just by choosing a sharp metric.

There's also a resolution issue. If your test set is small, you literally can't measure small probabilities of success, so everything below some threshold reads as zero. That makes the jump look more abrupt than it is.

I want to be careful about what we're not saying. We're not claiming large models can't do things small models can't. They clearly can. And we're not proving emergence is impossible in principle. Some capabilities might involve genuine qualitative shifts. Our point is that sharp, unpredictable jumps shouldn't be taken as evidence of something fundamental until you've ruled out the measurement explanation.

There's a practical upside, too. If much of this is smooth underneath, it's more predictable than we feared. You can pick metrics that track the underlying competence and forecast how capabilities will grow, which is useful for both science and safety.

r001.rationale: The response says many reported emergence effects depend on measurement, but does not state that emergence can always be removed by changing the metric or frame it as a metric-specific label.

r002.rationale: It cautions that sharp jumps should not be treated as evidence of a fundamental property until measurement effects are ruled out, and says genuine shifts remain possible.

r003.rationale: It mentions implications for safety and planning, but does not ask whether the field’s emphasis on emergence depends on whether it is fundamental.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, the headline claim around emergence was that as you scale these models up, certain capabilities appear suddenly and unpredictably. Below some threshold the model essentially can't do the task, and then past it, performance jumps. That's an exciting story, and it's also a slightly scary one, because it implies you can't forecast what a bigger model will be able to do.

What we found when we dug into it is that a lot of those sharp transitions are really artifacts of the metric, not the model. Think about exact-match accuracy on multi-digit arithmetic. The model has to get every single digit right to get any credit at all. So if the model is gradually getting better at predicting each digit, the per-token probability of the correct answer is improving smoothly with scale, but the all-or-nothing metric stays near zero and then shoots up once the model crosses the point where it gets all the digits right most of the time. The nonlinearity is in the scoring rule. If you swap in a continuous measure, like token edit distance or the log-likelihood of the correct answer, the curve looks smooth and predictable.

The second piece is resolution. A lot of these benchmarks have small test sets, so when the model is only correct one percent of the time, you can't see it. Zero is indistinguishable from one percent until you have enough examples. When you increase the test set size, the apparent discontinuity tends to go away as well.

And then we did what I think is the fun part, which is show you can manufacture emergence in vision models, where nobody had claimed it exists, just by picking a discontinuous metric. That convinced me it's a property of the measurement pipeline more than something deep about the networks.

Now, I want to be careful not to overclaim in the other direction. We're not saying models don't acquire new capabilities with scale. They clearly do. And there may be genuine phase transitions in some settings, things like grokking or in-context learning circuits look like candidates. What we're saying is that the evidence for sudden, unpredictable emergence is much weaker than it looked, and that the burden should be on showing the jump survives a change in metric. If it doesn't, you've learned something about your evaluation rather than about the model.

The practical upshot for me is about predictability and safety. If capabilities scale smoothly under the right measure, that's good news, because it means we can forecast and plan, rather than being surprised. So choosing metrics that reflect how the model is actually improving isn't just a methodological nicety, it changes what conclusions you draw about the whole scaling story.

r001.rationale: The response says many apparent sharp transitions are artifacts of the metric, can disappear under continuous measures, and reflect the measurement pipeline more than the networks. This conveys that emergence may be metric-dependent rather than fundamental.

r002.rationale: It explicitly cautions against overclaiming, noting that models do gain capabilities with scale and that genuine phase transitions may occur in some settings.

r003.rationale: The response discusses emergence’s implications for predictability and safety, but does not ask whether the field’s emphasis on emergence depends on it being fundamental.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate two things. One is whether the model is acquiring interesting capabilities as we scale it. The other is whether those capabilities appear suddenly, and that second claim can depend quite a lot on how you measure them.

Suppose you evaluate a task where the model only gets credit if the entire answer is correct. Its predictions could be improving smoothly, but your metric stays near zero until it crosses a threshold. Then you see this jump, and it looks like a new capability emerged. If you instead measure partial credit or the probability assigned to the correct answer, you might see a much smoother progression.

That doesn’t mean the capability isn’t real, or that every example of emergence is a measurement artifact. It means that a sudden jump in a benchmark score isn’t, by itself, evidence of a fundamental phase transition. You want to ask whether that conclusion holds across reasonable ways of measuring the same ability.

So I would treat emergence as something to investigate carefully, rather than an explanation. What changed in the model, what changed in the score, and can we distinguish those two things?

r001.rationale: The response says apparent jumps can depend on the metric, but does not state that if emergence can always be removed by changing the metric, it is a metric-specific label rather than a fundamental property.

r002.rationale: It cautions that a sudden benchmark jump alone does not establish a fundamental phase transition and says to check whether the conclusion holds across reasonable measurements.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask whether the importance the field places on emergence depends on emergence being fundamental.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two questions. One is whether the model’s capabilities are changing as we scale it up. The other is whether those changes are sudden. And the answer to that second question can depend quite a bit on how you measure performance.

For example, if you score a task as correct only when the model gets the entire answer right, you might see essentially zero performance and then a sharp jump. But if you look at partial credit, or the probability the model assigns to the right answer, you might see improvement happening much more smoothly. The underlying model hasn’t changed between those evaluations; the metric has.

That doesn’t mean there can’t be genuinely abrupt changes. It means that a jump on a benchmark isn’t, by itself, enough evidence to establish one. You want to ask whether that behavior persists across reasonable ways of measuring the capability. So I’d treat emergence as something to investigate carefully, rather than assume every surprising capability is a fundamental phase transition.
